passage:
Note to Ujjwal's parents, from Hansa, kindergarten teacher
Today Ujjwal told a visiting uncle, "Your cat drawing looks like a potato." He wasn't being cruel; he looked puzzled when the uncle's smile slipped. At line-up he would not let two older boys cut in. "That's not fair. We were here first." He stood his ground even when they glared. We practised saying a true thing in a kinder way: "I think the cat needs pointy ears." He tried it twice, grinning. His honesty and grit are real strengths; the tone is what we are working on together.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say the visiting uncle's cat drawing looked like?
qa.a: He said it looks like a potato.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's puzzled look suggest when the uncle's smile slipped?
qa.a: It suggests he said what he honestly thought and didn't expect it to hurt.

qa.q: What did Hansa try with Ujjwal after the potato comment?
qa.a: Hansa practised saying the same true thing more kindly, like suggesting pointy ears, and he tried it twice.

qa.q: How might the two older boys see Ujjwal after he stopped them cutting in?
qa.a: They may be annoyed, but they also learn he will not give way when something is unfair.

grounding: A teacher notes a blunt, fairness-minded young child and guides him toward a kinder tone without crushing his honesty.

passage: At the weekly haat, six-year-old Sachin watched the man weighing their onions. "Your scale is crooked," he announced. His elder brother Vijay went red. The seller laughed and checked it; the pan was sticking. On the walk home Vijay split the guavas: three for himself, two for Sachin. Sachin stopped in the dusty road. "That's not fair. You always take more." "I'm older." "Older doesn't eat more guavas." When Vijay walked on, Sachin sat down. Finally Vijay gave him one. "You're right," he said, "but say it without shouting next time." Sachin thought. "Okay. Quieter. Still fair."

qa.q: What did Sachin say about the seller's scale?
Why did Sachin sit down in the dusty road?
qa.a: He felt strongly that the guava split was unfair and was determined not to give way.

qa.q: What did Vijay ask Sachin to change, and how did Sachin respond?
qa.a: Vijay agreed he was right but asked him not to shout; Sachin agreed to be quieter but still fair.

qa.q: How did Vijay feel when Sachin called out the seller's scale?
qa.a: He went red, so he was probably embarrassed, even though Sachin turned out to be right.

grounding: A six-year-old says exactly what he thinks and argues for fairness, and his brother guides him toward a gentler tone.
